h: A famously overstuffed walrus and a garden full of sound
p: Every Horniman fan has a soft spot for the walrus. Stuffed in Victorian times by taxidermists who had probably never seen a live one, he was filled out so much that his natural wrinkles and folds disappeared, leaving a rather plump, smooth-looking beast. He's become the museum's unofficial mascot and sits proudly in the natural history gallery, usually surrounded by children.

The musical instrument collection is another highlight. There are hundreds of instruments from all over the world, and in the music gallery you can listen to many of them being played. Some spaces let visitors have a go themselves, which tends to be noisy and joyful in equal measure.

Out in the gardens, the Sound Garden has large outdoor instruments that anyone can play, and the Animal Walk is home to friendly creatures such as goats, sheep and alpacas. There's also a Victorian conservatory, a bandstand with views across London and a distinctive totem pole near the entrance. On a fine day, it's easy to spend as much time outside as you do inside.

Allow at least half a day if you plan to explore both the museum and the grounds. Forest Hill station is just a few minutes' walk away. Nearby, Dulwich Picture Gallery is a short trip for anyone who loves art, Sydenham Hill Wood is a lovely patch of ancient woodland for a ramble, and the famous Victorian dinosaur sculptures in Crystal Palace Park are a short bus ride away.
